newsitem.title: USA: U.S. natural jobless rate may decline -- W.House.
newsitem.headline: U.S. natural jobless rate may decline -- W.House.

text.p: The level of unemployment that can be sustained in the United States without putting upward pressure on inflation has fallen and may continue to decline in coming years, the White House said Monday.

In the annual Economic Report of the President, the White House said many factors, such as increased competition in labor and product markets, have led to a decline in the so-called "natural" jobless rate or non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU).
"A number of factors may continue to reduce the NAIRU in the future," said the report, which was prepared by the President's Council of Economic Advisers.

The White House cited demographic factors that would tend to lower the NAIRU. It pointed out that the current bulge of workers aged from 25 to 54 is moving into the 55-plus age bracket, where unemployment is typically lower.
Sustained unemployment in the United States itself is another reason the NAIRU could fall further, as such conditions mean workers' skills stay up-to-date, contributing to higher productivity.
The U.S. unemployment now stands at 5.4 percent.
Until recently, economists generally believed the natural jobless rate in the United States was around 6 percent.
However, after unemployment has remained below that level for two-and-half years without causing a pickup in inflation, many experts have concluded the natural rate has fallen.

Looking at the overall inflation picture, the White House predicted that the Consumer Price Index would edge lower and said it would be possible for real wages to increase without pushing the CPI higher.

"With continued growth of productivity with sustainable wage growth and with high profits as a buffer, the U.S. economy has room for a sustained increase in real wages -- without rising inflation," the White House report said.
